section.title: The Judge of the Earth
section.sectionRationale: An imprecatory psalm indicting corrupt human rulers who pervert justice, described as estranged from the womb and venomous as a deaf serpent. David prays boldly for God to break their power, and the psalm closes not in personal vengeance but in the settled conviction that there is a God who judges the earth.
section.thesis: Against corrupt rulers who pervert justice from birth, David prays boldly for God to break their power, confident that history will end with one settled verdict: there is a God who judges the earth, a verdict finally and fully rendered at the return of Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the indictment of corrupt judges who speak injustice; the depth of the wicked's corruption, pictured as a deaf, venomous serpent; the bold imprecatory prayer for God to break their power; and the closing vindication, surely there is a God who judges the earth.

units.label: Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers

verses.text: Do you indeed speak justly, O rulers? Do you judge uprightly, O sons of men?
No, in your hearts you devise {{avel|injustice}}; with your hands you mete out violence on the earth.

units.label: Estranged from the womb
units.note: the depth of the wicked's corruption

verses.text: The wicked are estranged from the womb; the liars go astray from birth.
Their venom is like the venom of a snake, like a cobra that shuts its ears,
refusing to hear the tune of the charmer who skillfully weaves his spell.
O God, shatter their teeth in their mouths; O LORD, tear out the fangs of the lions.
May they vanish like water that runs off; when they draw the bow, may their arrows be blunted.

Like a slug that dissolves in its slime, like a woman’s stillborn child, 
may they never see the sun.

Before your pots can feel the burning thorns, whether green or dry, 
He will sweep them away.

units.label: Surely there is a God who judges the earth

verses.text: The righteous will rejoice when they see they are avenged; they will wash their feet in the blood of the wicked.

Then men will say, “There is surely a reward for the righteous! 
There is surely a {{shaphat|God who judges}} the earth!”

avel.gloss: Injustice, unrighteousness, moral wrong. The rulers indicted here have devised avel in their very hearts before ever acting, showing that the corruption of unjust judgment begins internally, in intention, before it is carried out in violence.

shaphat.gloss: To judge, to govern, to render a verdict. The psalm's closing declaration, there is surely a God who judges the earth, uses this same root that describes human rulers in verse 1, contrasting their failed, corrupt judgment with God's own perfect and final judgment.

basic.context: This psalm confronts corrupt human rulers directly, those entrusted with justice who instead devise violence in their hearts. David describes their corruption as running so deep it seems present from birth, like the venom of a snake that refuses even the charmer's skill. He then prays boldly, even violently, for God to break their power, using vivid images of broken teeth, melting slugs, and stillborn children. The psalm closes not in personal triumph but in a settled theological conclusion: there is a God who judges the earth.
basic.hermeneutics: This is an imprecatory psalm, and its harsh language should be read as honest, Spirit-inspired prayer appealing to God's own justice against real, entrenched corruption in those who hold power, not as personal vengeance for private grievance. The psalmist does not act against the wicked himself; he hands the whole matter to God, the only one with the right and the ability to judge the earth justly.
basic.originalLanguages: The rulers indicted in verse 2 devise avel, injustice, internally, in their hearts, before it ever surfaces in violent action. The psalm's closing declaration uses shaphat, judge, the very verb describing the corrupt human rulers of verse 1, contrasting their failed judgment with God's perfect and final verdict over all the earth.
basic.typology: The psalm's demand that corrupt judges be finally overturned and that a righteous verdict be rendered over the whole earth anticipates the final judgment, when Christ, the only truly righteous Judge, will set every wrong right and vindicate the oppressed completely.
basic.christ: This psalm's imprecations are not personal revenge but appeals to God as the only righteous Judge, a posture the New Testament commends explicitly, leave room for God's wrath, for it is written, vengeance is Mine, I will repay, says the Lord, Romans 12:19. The psalm's closing hope, there is surely a God who judges the earth, is fulfilled in Jesus Christ, to whom the Father has given all authority to judge, and who has fixed a day on which He will judge the world in righteousness, Acts 17:31, finally silencing every unjust mouth and vindicating every oppressed soul, Revelation 20:11-15.
basic.god: God is shown as the only truly righteous Judge, in stark contrast to corrupt human rulers who pervert justice from birth. His judgment, though the psalm prays for it urgently and vividly, is not capricious but perfectly aligned with true righteousness, and it will be rendered with certainty over the whole earth.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 12:19 instructs believers to leave vengeance to God rather than take it themselves. Acts 17:31 declares that God has fixed a day on which He will judge the world in righteousness through Jesus Christ. Revelation 20:11-15 pictures the final judgment before God's great white throne, when every unjust deed is finally accounted for.
basic.oneStory: Against corrupt rulers who twist justice from birth, this psalm prays boldly that God alone would judge and set things right, closing in the settled conviction that there is a God who judges the earth. That conviction is fulfilled in Jesus Christ, given all authority to judge, who will finally and completely vindicate the righteous and silence every unjust mouth.

context.literary:
Psalm 58 is built as a courtroom in reverse. It opens with a question put to the judges (verse 1), moves to the charge and the evidence (verses 2 to 5), turns to petition (verses 6 to 9), and ends with the verdict of onlookers (verses 10 to 11). The defendants are never given the floor. They are addressed in the second person only once, in verse 1, and from then on they are spoken about, as if the psalmist has decided they will not listen, which is exactly what verses 4 and 5 say of them.

The middle of the psalm is a run of similes, and the pace is deliberate. In verses 4 to 5 the wicked are a cobra with its ears stopped. In verse 6 they are lions, in verse 7 water that drains away, in the same verse an archer whose arrows go blunt, in verse 8 a slug and a stillborn child, and in verse 9 a cooking fire that gets to the pot before the thorns have properly caught. No image is allowed to settle. The effect is of a mind reaching for every picture of helplessness it can find for the people who looked so powerful in verse 2.

There is also a quiet contrast between mouths and hands, between speech and action. The rulers are asked whether they speak justly, yet their hearts devise and their hands deal out violence (verse 2). Their venom is in the mouth (verse 4) and the prayer asks for teeth broken in the mouth (verse 6). What they did with speech and power is undone at the very place they did it. The closing verse then hands the last word to ordinary people, who say what they have seen: there is a reward for the righteous, and there is a God who judges.

The psalm sits in a group of four with the same heading, Psalms 56 to 59 (with 57, 58 and 59 also carrying the tune marking Do Not Destroy), all prayers of David under threat from men of power, and it is the sharpest of them in tone.
context.historical:
In Israel's world, justice was not chiefly a matter of courts in a building. Elders sat in the city gate, the king was the final judge, and the law commanded that judges be appointed in every town to judge the people with righteous judgment (Deuteronomy 16:18-20). The same passage forbids perverting justice, showing partiality, or taking a bribe, for a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise. Those were the very temptations the psalm has in view. A poor man with no patron had nowhere else to go, so a bent judge was a particular kind of danger, because the one place meant to protect the weak had become the place that crushed them. The prophets later describe the same abuse in the same terms, for example Isaiah 10:1-2 and Micah 3:1-3.

The psalm is headed as David's, and the neighbouring psalms tie him to the years of flight from Saul, when David saw at close range what a king and his officials could do with power. Judges and officers who served a hostile court, or who looked on while the innocent were pursued, are a natural fit, though the psalm itself names no one and so was always free to be prayed against any corrupt bench.

The snake imagery would have been familiar to hearers who knew the desert. Snake charming was a recognised trade, and Ecclesiastes 10:11 speaks of a snake that bites before it is charmed, and Jeremiah 8:17 speaks of vipers that cannot be charmed. A cobra that cannot be charmed is a dangerous animal with nothing to appeal to. The picture of the wicked as a snake that will not listen is therefore not decoration but a judgment that there is no longer any point in arguing with them.

Washing the feet in blood (verse 10) is the language of a battlefield after a victory. Psalm 68:23 uses the same kind of picture, and Isaiah 63:1-6 pictures God Himself as a warrior stained with the blood of His enemies. A first hearer would take it as the vivid shorthand of victory, not as a scene the righteous were expected to relish.
context.canonical:
The psalm belongs to a thread in the Psalter that asks God to rise as judge. Psalm 94:1-2 calls Him the God of vengeance and the Judge of the earth, and Psalm 82 shows the same scene from the heavenly side: God presides in the divine assembly and asks, 'How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked?' (Psalm 82:1-2). Psalm 58:11 closes on a statement that sounds like the answer to that question, that there is a God who judges in the earth. Abraham had used the same conviction centuries before, appealing to it when he asked, 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?' (Genesis 18:25).

Verses 3 to 5 draw on the garden story. The serpent of Genesis 3 is the original deceiver, and the serpent language here belongs to that family. The psalm's confession that the wicked are estranged from the womb stands beside David's own confession in Psalm 51:5, that he was brought forth in iniquity. Both make sin older than any single act.

The New Testament takes up the snake language against religious leaders who had the same problem. John the Baptist and Jesus both call them a brood of vipers (Matthew 3:7; Matthew 23:33). Paul's chain of quotations about the human throat and lips in Romans 3:13 draws on Psalm 140:3, a close cousin of Psalm 58's venom. The cry for justice passes into the book of Revelation, where the martyrs ask 'How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood and judge those who dwell upon the earth?' (Revelation 6:10). When that judgment arrives, heaven's response is the one this psalm anticipates: 'Hallelujah! ... His judgments are true and just' (Revelation 19:1-2), and Revelation 18:20 calls on the saints to rejoice because God has pronounced judgment for them. The psalm's closing scene is therefore not left hanging; the New Testament shows where it ends.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wanted the godly to know that they are allowed to name injustice plainly and to bring it, at full strength, to God. The psalm does not soften its verdict on the judges. It says they are guilty in the heart before they are guilty in the hand, and it says this to the ones who most needed to hear it, since they were the guardians of the law. Hearers who were suffering under a crooked court were meant to learn that their anger was not a fault to be hidden but a prayer to be offered.

He also meant to teach restraint by example. Everything the psalm wants to happen to the wicked is put in the form of a request to God. Not one line describes the psalmist doing anything to them. The cursing is speech directed upward and the wrath is handed over, which is exactly how the New Testament later says believers should treat their enemies.

And he meant the psalm to end in public knowledge. The last verse gives the voice to 'men', people in general, who look at what has happened and draw the conclusion the corrupt judges had denied. The psalm is aimed at making it plain, before an audience, that the world is governed by a just God and that goodness is not wasted.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records a prayer. It is not a command to curse, and it is not a programme of action. Nothing in it tells Israel to break anyone's teeth or to shed blood, and nothing tells the godly to rejoice over suffering as such. The feet in blood of verse 10 is a picture of victory that belongs to the psalm's poetry and to God's own act, not an instruction.

What does carry over is a pattern of praying. The believer is invited to speak honestly about what officials and institutions have done, to ask God to act as judge, and to leave the action with Him, as Romans 12:19 says: vengeance belongs to the Lord. Jesus did not cancel that honesty. He told His followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them (Matthew 5:44), and on the cross He prayed for the men who crucified Him (Luke 23:34). A Christian praying this psalm prays it with both in view: a hunger for justice that is real, and a mercy toward people that is also real, leaving the final verdict with the One whose verdicts are true. It also helps to remember that the psalm is sung by the powerless. Reading it from the seat of power would turn a cry for rescue into a licence for cruelty, which is the reverse of what it teaches.

debates.question: Who are the 'rulers' of verse 1?

views.label: Human judges and officials
views.case: The parallel line says 'sons of men', and the charge is about what 'the earth' suffers from their hands. The BSB reads it this way. This fits the concern for courts in Deuteronomy 16:18-20 and the prophets' attacks on judges, and verse 2 speaks of hearts and hands, which are human.

views.label: Divine beings who govern the nations
views.case: The Hebrew consonants of the opening word can be read in more than one way, and the traditional pointing and some ancient versions differ. Some read it as 'gods', which would link the psalm to Psalm 82, where God judges the gods who judged unjustly. Verse 11, which says God judges, then reads as the answer to lesser powers.

views.label: Human rulers called by a divine title
views.case: Others keep the human setting and recall that in Psalm 82:6 the judges are addressed as gods because they act in His name, only to be told they will die like mortals. The rulers are then addressed as those who hold God's authority and have abused it.

debates.bearing: Every reading arrives at the same place: those who hold authority are answerable to a higher Judge. Whether the psalm addresses people or powers behind them, its prayer and its confidence are the same, and the New Testament is at home with both (Ephesians 6:12).

debates.question: How can a Christian pray the harsher lines of verses 6 to 9?

views.label: As a prayer that God would end the wicked power
views.case: The requests are aimed at the power to harm: teeth, fangs, bows. On this view the psalm asks that injustice be stopped and that the victims be freed, and it does not ask for gloating cruelty. Jesus Himself pronounces woe and judgment on hypocritical rulers (Matthew 23:33).

views.label: As prophecy of God's judgment, sung in Christ
views.case: Many in the church's tradition have read such psalms as words that speak of what God will do and that find their truth in Christ, who will judge the living and the dead. Revelation 6:10 and 19:1-2 put similar cries into heaven.

views.label: As words the Old Testament could say but the new covenant reshapes
views.case: Another view holds that the psalm's imagery belongs to a covenant setting with earthly kings and battles, and that after the cross the church is told to bless its persecutors and to fight the powers with the gospel (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:21).

debates.bearing: The three readings agree on the boundaries: the prayer is directed to God, it is not a licence to do harm, and it is tempered by the call to forgive. Praying the psalm keeps alive both a hatred of injustice and a readiness to see its doers repent, which is why Jesus could both lament over a city and warn it.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 opens with a word that translators handle in different ways. The BSB has 'rulers'. The Hebrew consonants can be read as a word meaning 'silence' (the older English rendering 'O congregation' follows this family of readings) or as the plural of the word for 'gods'. The verse therefore rests on a real textual and grammatical question, discussed in the debate above, and it is worth holding lightly which reading is meant.

In verse 2 the wicked 'devise' injustice in the heart, and their hands 'mete out' violence. The second verb belongs to the language of weighing, the picture of someone measuring out a portion on scales. The word for violence, chamas, is the same word used of the earth being filled with violence before the flood in Genesis 6:11. A scale that should be set to give every person what is fair has been rigged to hand out harm, and the psalm picks the image on purpose, because a judge's whole work is to weigh.

Verse 3 says the wicked are 'estranged'. The verb is zur, to turn aside, and it is the root behind the ordinary word for a stranger, zar. The wicked have become strangers to God from the womb, which goes further than saying they have done wrong: they belong outside the family. Verse 4 picks up a word with two sides. Chemah can mean venom, as in Deuteronomy 32:33, 'the venom of serpents, the deadly poison of cobras', and it can also mean heat or rage. The cobra here is the peten, the hooded snake that Isaiah 11:8 knows as the creature a child must not reach for. The charmer of verse 5 is a 'whisperer', a word built on a root for muttering spells, matching the inaudible incantation of Ecclesiastes 10:11.

In verse 6 the lions' fangs are pictured as the tearing teeth of a beast, and the verb 'tear out' is a violent one. Verse 8 offers a puzzle: the word for slug occurs in a verse whose Hebrew is hard, and the word for the stillborn child, nephel, appears in Job 3:16 and Ecclesiastes 6:3 as the picture of a life that never saw daylight. Verse 9 is among the hardest verses in the Psalter to translate, and modern versions differ widely; it is safest to read it as a picture of sudden removal.

Verse 11 has a striking phrase. The 'reward' for the righteous is literally 'fruit', the word peri. The righteous are not promised an abstract payment but a harvest. The second half says there is a God who judges 'in the earth', and the word for judges is a plural participle, matching the earlier plural of verse 1. The verb is the same one, shaphat, that names what the human judges were supposed to do, so the last line turns the opening question around: the ones who were asked whether they judged justly are now judged.

typology.type: The judge who is judged, verses 1 and 11
typology.fulfillment: The psalm sets human judges under a divine Judge who sees their hearts, and Israel's hope was always for a king who would judge rightly. Isaiah says of the coming Shoot from Jesse that 'with righteousness He will judge the poor, and with equity He will decide for the lowly of the earth' (Isaiah 11:4). In Christ that hope takes flesh, for Acts 17:31 says God has fixed a day to judge the world in righteousness by the Man He has appointed. The difference is that Jesus was Himself once judged by unjust rulers. Pilate and the council perverted justice against Him, and in rising He showed that the verdict of heaven is the one that stands.

typology.type: The serpent who will not be charmed, verses 4 and 5
typology.fulfillment: The snake imagery looks back to Genesis 3:1, where the serpent's craftiness ruined the first home, and forward to the promise that the woman's offspring will crush the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15). Jesus turns the image on rulers who refused every appeal, calling them a brood of vipers (Matthew 23:33). The final fulfilment is that the old serpent is himself judged, cast down as Revelation 12:9 and 20:10 describe. The type stops short in this way: the psalm sees deafness to correction in a group of people, while the New Testament shows the deeper source of it and the deeper remedy, a rescue that can reach even stopped ears (Acts 9:1-6).

typology.type: The righteous who see vindication, verses 10 and 11
typology.fulfillment: The psalm closes with the godly rejoicing because they have seen God act. Revelation gives the scene its full size: the martyrs who cried 'How long?' (Revelation 6:10) are answered when a great multitude cries 'Hallelujah! ... His judgments are true and just' (Revelation 19:1-2), and the saints are told to rejoice over a fallen Babylon because God has judged for them (Revelation 18:20). The fulfilment surpasses the type because the Lamb who was slain is the one who opens the book and judges, and because the final rejoicing belongs to a people gathered from every nation and not to a single faction. The bloodstained feet, meanwhile, give way to a picture of Christ's own blood as the means by which mercy, and not only judgment, is offered (Romans 5:9).

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by longing. It describes a world in which the courts cannot be trusted and then declares that there is a God who judges. The Old Testament never lets that hope float free of a person. Isaiah says of the coming King that 'with righteousness He will judge the poor, and with equity He will decide for the lowly of the earth' and that 'righteousness will be the belt around His hips' (Isaiah 11:4-5). Peter's preaching and Paul's at Athens make it explicit that the judge God has appointed is Jesus (Acts 10:42; Acts 17:31). The psalm's last verse asked for a Judge, and the gospel names Him.

It leads to Christ by contrast. The rulers of the psalm speak injustice and hand out violence. The night Jesus was arrested, He stood before rulers who did exactly that, and Matthew 26 to 27 shows the council seeking false testimony and Pilate giving way to a crowd. The Judge of all the earth stood in the dock and took the sentence that belonged to the guilty. That is why the final outcome of Psalm 58 cannot be separated from the cross: God does not merely overturn unjust verdicts; in Christ He takes the just penalty for sin upon Himself, so that mercy and justice meet (Romans 3:25-26).

It leads to Christ by pattern of response. The psalmist hands vengeance over. Jesus did not retaliate when He was insulted and entrusted Himself to the One who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23). He prayed, 'Father, forgive them' (Luke 23:34), and He taught His followers to love their enemies (Matthew 5:44). Yet He did not abandon the psalm's conviction. He spoke of a day when the Son of Man would come and there would be judgment, and He told of a widow who pleaded with an unjust judge and was granted justice, adding that God will promptly carry out justice for His elect who cry to Him day and night (Luke 18:7-8).

Finally, the serpent in this psalm is the serpent of Genesis 3, and the promise of Genesis 3:15 is what makes the wicked's boasting hollow. Paul says that at the cross Christ disarmed the powers and authorities and made a public spectacle of them (Colossians 2:15). The psalm's broken teeth and blunted arrows, read in this light, are a picture of what happened at the cross and of what will be completed when He returns. A caution keeps the reading honest: the psalm's particular images, the slug, the pots and the thorns, are not each a coded picture of Christ. What leads to Him is its cry for a righteous Judge and its confidence that one exists.
study.god:
The psalm shows a God who is judge before He is anything else in this scene, and it is careful about what kind. He is not an angry power who happens to be strong. He is the one who weighs, and the closing word is that there is a reward for the righteous. Psalm 7:11 says that God is a righteous judge, and the same conviction underlies this psalm: His anger is not a flaw in Him but the other side of His love for what is right and for the people who are harmed.

The psalm also shows that God is near enough to be addressed. The verbs of verse 6 are put directly to Him, 'O God... O LORD', using both the general and the covenant name. The prayer assumes He hears, and the reason He can be asked to act on behalf of the powerless is that He has already placed Himself on their side. The law that He gave commands justice for the widow, the orphan and the stranger, and the prophets repeat it. A God who is the judge of the earth is also the defender of people the earth ignores.

There is a tension the psalm holds without resolving. God's judgment is certain, and yet the psalm asks Him to act, and the prayer itself is part of how it comes about. Both are true: He is the judge of all the earth whose verdicts do not depend on anyone's request (Genesis 18:25), and He invites His people to call on Him for justice (Luke 18:7). The psalm also holds together God's fierceness and His patience. Elsewhere Scripture says that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11), and the New Testament says His patience is meant to lead to repentance (2 Peter 3:9). This psalm does not deny that; it speaks for those who have waited a long time and asks how long.

For worship, the psalm teaches that praise includes the truth that God puts things right. The last two verses are what believers say when they see justice done: 'There is surely a reward for the righteous! There is surely a God who judges the earth!' A church that never sings about His justice is missing half of what the psalm sings. It also humbles the listener. Because God alone has the right to judge, every human verdict is provisional, including our own, and the right response to the psalm is to hand our grievances to Him and to ask that He also search our own hearts (Psalm 139:23-24).

crossReferences.note: The law's own charge to judges: appoint them in every town, do not pervert justice, show no partiality, take no bribe. Psalm 58 is the indictment of judges who did the opposite, and it shows the standard against which their hearts and hands are measured.

God presides in the divine assembly and asks, 'How long will you judge unjustly and show partiality to the wicked?' The psalm is a close companion to Psalm 58, whether or not the rulers of Psalm 58:1 are read as divine beings, for both set corrupt judgment under the judgment of God.

They sharpen their tongues like snakes, with the venom of vipers on their lips. The same snake picture for wicked speech appears here in another prayer of David, and Paul draws on it in Romans 3:13, which shows that the snake language was taken as a description of human sin generally.

David confesses that he himself was brought forth in iniquity. Set beside Psalm 58:3, it stops the psalm from being read as the righteous pointing at others: the same inherited corruption is owned by the psalmist, which is why he trusts God's verdict and not his own.

'O LORD, God of vengeance... Rise up, O Judge of the earth; render a reward to the proud.' It is another prayer that asks God to do openly what the wicked have denied, and it shares Psalm 58's title for God as Judge of the earth.
Abraham's question, 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?', is the conviction behind Psalm 58:11. The psalm's final line is the answer that history gives to Abraham's question.

Paul tells believers not to take revenge but to leave room for God's wrath, because vengeance is His. It gives the New Testament's reading of how Psalm 58 is to be prayed: honestly, but with the verdict left in God's hands.

Jesus calls the scribes and Pharisees a 'brood of vipers' and asks how they will escape the sentence of hell. He applies the psalm's snake picture to religious rulers who had power over the people and used it badly, and so shows the psalm is not simply an Old Testament harshness.

The martyrs cry, 'How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood and judge those who dwell upon the earth?' It is the psalm's prayer in heaven, showing that the longing for God to judge belongs to the people of Christ and is answered in the end.

'His judgments are true and just.' A great multitude rejoices over the judgment that the psalm asked for. It is the fulfilment of the last two verses of Psalm 58, where the righteous see what God has done and declare there is a God who judges the earth.

study.oneStory:
The psalm answers a question that begins in Genesis. When the first couple distrusted God's word, human authority was spoiled at its root, and the record that follows is full of rulers who use their power on the weak. Cain's answer to God in Genesis 4:9 already shows the pattern: a human being asked to account for his brother answers with a question of his own. By the time of the judges and kings, the law could list the duties of a judge in detail and still see them broken. Psalm 58 belongs to the long line of witnesses who say aloud what everyone has seen: the people in charge are not always just.

It sets up what follows by insisting that the last word is not with those people. The prophets repeat the theme, promising a king who will judge the poor with righteousness (Isaiah 11:3-5) and a day when God Himself will set the world right. The psalm's closing line anticipates the conviction that runs through the whole Bible, that the Judge of all the earth will do what is right (Genesis 18:25).

The story's centre is the cross. There the highest human court condemned the only truly righteous man, and God used that very verdict to carry the judgment the guilty deserve. Christ rose, and the one who was judged unjustly was appointed to judge the world in righteousness (Acts 17:31). The church between His resurrection and return still prays the psalm's prayer, as in Revelation 6:10, and it prays it while loving its enemies.

It ends in the new creation. Revelation 19:1-2 has a great multitude rejoicing that God's judgments are true and just, and Revelation 21:4 describes a world in which there is no more mourning, crying or pain. The rigged scales of Psalm 58:2 are replaced by the throne of God and of the Lamb (Revelation 22:3). In that city nobody needs a judge to rescue them from another human being, because 'No longer will there be any curse', and the righteous who once asked where justice was will see that the question has been answered for good.

quiz.q: Who does this psalm indict in its opening verses?

options.text: Rulers and judges who devise injustice and violence rather than judging uprightly.
options.note: Verses 1-2 directly address rulers who fail to speak justly or judge uprightly.

options.text: Foreign invading armies.
options.note: The indictment is against corrupt rulers or judges, not a foreign invading force.

options.text: Ordinary farmers and merchants.
options.note: The psalm's target is specifically those entrusted with rendering justice, not ordinary tradespeople.

options.text: Prophets who spoke false messages.
options.note: The indictment concerns rulers and judges, not prophetic figures specifically.

quiz.q: How does the psalm describe the depth of the wicked's corruption in verses 3-5?

options.text: As estranged from the womb, going astray from birth, like a snake that refuses to hear the charmer.
options.note: This vivid language describes corruption as deep-seated and resistant to correction, present from birth.

options.text: As a temporary lapse in otherwise good judgment.
options.note: The text describes deep, persistent corruption, not a minor or temporary lapse.

options.text: As caused entirely by poor education.
options.note: The psalm's imagery describes an inborn moral condition, not merely a lack of education.

options.text: As limited to only a few isolated individuals.
options.note: The description applies broadly to 'the wicked' as a category, not merely a rare few individuals.

quiz.q: How should the vivid imprecatory prayers of verses 6-9 be understood?

options.text: As honest, Spirit-inspired prayer appealing to God's own justice, not a model for personal vengeance.
options.note: Every verb of judgment in these verses is directed to God to act, not to David himself.

options.text: As direct instructions for believers to physically harm their enemies.
options.note: The prayers are addressed entirely to God to act; they are not instructions for personal violence.

options.text: As purely poetic language with no real theological content.
options.note: The prayers reflect a genuine theological conviction about God's justice, not merely empty poetic flourish.

options.text: As evidence that David had abandoned faith in God's justice.
options.note: The opposite is true; these prayers reflect deep faith that God alone can and will render justice.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's closing conclusion in verse 11?

options.text: There is surely a reward for the righteous, and a God who judges the earth.
options.note: This is the psalm's climactic, settled theological conclusion.

options.text: There is no hope for justice in this life or the next.
options.note: The psalm concludes with confident hope in God's justice, not despair.

options.text: The righteous must take justice into their own hands.
options.note: The psalm consistently entrusts judgment to God, not to human self-action.

options.text: Corrupt rulers will always escape judgment.
options.note: The psalm's conclusion is the opposite: God will judge, and the righteous will see it.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's longing for justice find its fulfillment in the New Testament?

options.text: In Jesus Christ, to whom the Father has given all authority to judge the world in righteousness.
options.note: Acts 17:31 directly ties final, righteous judgment of the whole earth to Jesus Christ.

options.text: In the complete abolition of any future judgment.
options.note: The New Testament affirms a coming final judgment, not its abolition.

options.text: In teaching that all human rulers are equally righteous.
options.note: This is not the New Testament's teaching; corrupt human authority remains a real problem addressed by final divine judgment.

options.text: In encouraging believers to personally overthrow unjust rulers by force.
options.note: The New Testament, like this psalm, entrusts final judgment to God, not to violent personal or political overthrow.

questions: This psalm indicts leaders who use their position for injustice rather than righteousness. Where do you see corrupted power in the world today, and how does this psalm shape the way you pray about it?

The psalm describes the wicked's corruption as deep-seated, resistant even to skilled correction. How does this sober picture of sin's depth shape your understanding of your own need for God's grace, not just moral effort?

This psalm's harsh prayers are directed entirely to God to act, never instructing David to take vengeance himself. Where do you need to consciously hand a desire for justice or revenge over to God rather than acting on it yourself?
The psalm closes with confidence that there is a God who judges the earth. How does trusting in a final, certain judgment change the way you respond to injustice you cannot currently fix?
Jesus is given all authority to judge the world in righteousness. How does knowing that final judgment belongs entirely to Christ free you from needing to personally settle every score in this life?

translationNotes.note: Some translations render 'O rulers' as 'O gods' or 'O mighty ones,' reflecting an ambiguous Hebrew term (elem) that may address human judges functioning in a God-given role of authority, or possibly divine council imagery; either reading points to those entrusted with rendering justice.
Like a woman's stillborn child is a stark ancient Near Eastern image for something that never reaches its intended purpose or maturity, applied here to the wicked's schemes coming to nothing.

Wash their feet in the blood of the wicked is hyperbolic ancient Near Eastern imagery for a decisive, total victory and vindication, not a literal prescription for believers' conduct toward the defeated.
